1425.bp: Over 932,000 people speak Tetun in Timor-Leste, yet AI-powered conversational tools—the kind that let you ask questions and get helpful answers—were built almost entirely for English and other languages spoken by billions. This matters because speakers of smaller languages get cut off from useful AI services that others take for granted, keeping them at a disadvantage in the digital economy.
1425.wh: AI conversational assistants are trained on vast amounts of text from the internet, which means they've absorbed millions of examples of English and Mandarin but only scraps of Tetun. When these systems try to answer questions in Tetun, they often produce nonsense or ignore what speakers actually need, because the system hasn't learned the patterns of how Tetun questions should be answered. The obvious approach of just scaling up the LLM doesn't fix this—you still need the assistant to know what Tetun-speaking communities actually care about.
1425.ap: The researchers took existing AI conversational systems and adapted them specifically for Tetun by crafting instruction prompts that teach the model how Tetun speakers pose questions and what kinds of answers matter to them. This is essentially giving the model a cultural primer in how to be useful to Tetun speakers, rather than forcing Tetun into English-shaped communication patterns.
1425.ww: When you show an AI system examples of how real Tetun speakers communicate and what they find helpful, the system learns to anticipate their needs and generate answers that fit their context, not just generic responses in the right language. This targeted approach works because the system is now being steered by the actual patterns of what Tetun-speaking users care about.
1425.po: User studies found that 91% of tasks completed successfully and users rated satisfaction at 4.30 out of 5, demonstrating that language-specific customization actually delivers. The paper shows a practical playbook that any community speaking a small language can follow to unlock AI-powered services that aren't yet mainstream for them.

1426.bp: In today's job market, being visible on professional networks like LinkedIn can make or break your career—employers and collaborators find you through what you post. But most professionals lack the marketing skill to produce high-quality posts regularly, and when they turn to AI to help, they run into a frustrating wall: the AI produces generic, forgettable content that sounds like everyone else's.
1426.wh: Standard AI systems work by predicting the most statistically likely next word, which naturally pushes outputs toward the average and the common. When thousands of people are using the same AI assistant to write LinkedIn posts, everyone ends up with similar wording, similar examples, and similar tone. The result is 'lexical homogenization'—the feed becomes a sea of nearly identical AI-generated posts, and none of them stand out. An individual's unique expertise and personality get buried under statistical mediocrity.
1426.ap: SOMIN takes a different approach by building an 'agentic' system—one that plans multiple steps of content generation rather than just writing one post at a time. It uses dynamic retrieval, meaning it actively goes searching for fresh ideas and examples unique to your expertise and context, then uses those findings to generate a post that's grounded in real specifics about you, not generic patterns. The system works through planning (what angles to take), retrieval (finding relevant facts about you), and generation (writing a post that uses those specifics).
1426.ww: Because the system retrieves specific facts about your work and background before writing, the post ends up rooted in concrete details that are unique to you. This blocks the AI from sliding into generic phrasing—you can't sound like everyone else if your post is built on particular examples and achievements that only you have. The multi-step planning also means the system can explore different angles and pick the most interesting one.
1426.po: The paper demonstrates that agentic systems produce more distinctive, higher-performing content than single-prompt AI assistance. By bridging the gap between raw AI ability and the domain expertise that makes someone hireable, professionals can maintain a high-quality public presence without becoming a marketing specialist themselves.

1427.bp: Deep research—the work of finding answers by reading across dozens or hundreds of sources, cross-checking facts, and synthesizing a coherent report—is becoming increasingly important for AI systems and organizations. But doing deep research at scale, where you need to process thousands of similar research jobs in parallel, reveals a hard constraint: current AI assistants are designed to chat one-on-one, not to crunch batch jobs like a factory.
1427.wh: Today's AI assistants were built for interactive conversation where you talk to one agent at a time. That design makes sense for chat, but it doesn't map onto the needs of production workflows where you might need to analyze a thousand research questions at once. You can't efficiently run a thousand separate chat sessions in parallel; you need a system designed from the ground up for concurrent processing, the way data-processing systems are designed to handle millions of records at once.
1427.ap: C3Flow treats each AI agent as a scheduled, isolated worker in a factory line (following the SIMD—Single Instruction, Multiple Data—pattern from computer architecture). Each agent handles the same multi-step research task independently: retrieve evidence, read it, extract facts, check them, synthesize a report. The system logs every step of each agent's work and can route different tasks to different models if needed. Multiple agents run in parallel, so you can process batches of research jobs rather than one at a time.
1427.ww: By isolating each task as an independent unit and running them in parallel, the system bypasses the bottleneck of sequential chat. The logging means you can inspect what each agent did, debug failures, and understand which steps are slow. The system also gets to benefit from routing more complex tasks to stronger (or more expensive) models while using cheaper models for simpler parts—you can be strategic about where to spend compute.
1427.po: On one benchmark, C3Flow improved accuracy from 48.44% to 61.59% (a substantial jump) and handled a fact-checking task 5.9× faster than human annotators while maintaining 87.5% accuracy. This shows that the batch-processing approach unlocks both better results and dramatic speedup for large-scale research.

1428.bp: When AI systems answer questions, they need to ground their answers in real information from the internet or a database—otherwise they just guess. The gold standard approach (called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG) is to search for relevant documents first, then have the AI read those documents and answer based on what it found. The infrastructure for this already exists in academic research tools, but there's been a gap: those tools weren't designed to plug directly into AI assistants.
1428.wh: Researchers have built powerful toolkits like Pyserini (for searching) and RankLLM (for ranking search results by relevance) that academic labs use for information retrieval research. But AI assistants have their own world of tools and APIs. The two communities speak different languages, so researchers experimenting with how to make AI better at using search have to build bridges manually. There's no standard way to wire a research toolkit directly into an AI agent.
1428.ap: The paper presents MCP servers—adapters that follow an emerging industry standard called the Model Context Protocol. These adapters take the capabilities of Pyserini and RankLLM (sparse search, dense search, reranking, multimodal search) and expose them as callable tools that any AI assistant can invoke. An AI agent can now say 'search for this query' or 'rerank these results' and get back structured answers, the same way it might ask for the weather or a calculator result.
1428.ww: By following a standard protocol (MCP), the system becomes pluggable—any AI assistant that supports MCP can now use these research tools without custom integration code. This matters because it connects the academic IR research infrastructure (which has decades of refinement in search quality) to the emerging world of AI agents. Researchers can now quickly experiment with different retrieval and reranking approaches without rebuilding infrastructure.
1428.po: The paper demonstrates end-to-end workflows combining search, reranking, and reasoning across different AI models (open-source and proprietary). This is the bridge that lets researchers experiment with how AI and search should work together, accelerating progress on making AI-powered assistants more factual and grounded.

1429.bp: In peer review, scientists evaluate each other's work, and the fairness and quality of that review directly affects which ideas get published. But reviewers often make claims in their reviews that are opinions stated as facts, or criticisms that don't actually match what the paper says. There's no systematic way to audit whether a reviewer's claims are accurate, so unfair or careless reviews can influence publication decisions unchecked.
1429.wh: Peer reviews are long, dense documents, and checking every claim manually would require re-reading the original paper alongside each review and making judgment calls on dozens of statements. At a conference with hundreds of submissions, doing this manually is impossible. The obvious approach—having another human check—creates even more work and still requires expertise to judge edge cases.
1429.ap: Peerispect is a system that automatically extracts statements from peer reviews that are 'check-worthy' (claims about what the paper did, what results it achieved, whether a technique is sound). For each extracted claim, the system retrieves relevant passages from the manuscript and runs a natural language inference check—essentially asking 'does the paper actually support this claim?'. The results are shown in a visual interface where you can see the claim and the evidence highlighted in the original paper side by side.
1429.ww: By automating the extraction and retrieval steps, the system makes verification tractable at scale. A reviewer or program committee member can scan the claims and their supporting evidence in minutes instead of hours. The system doesn't make the final judgment (that's still human), but it does the laborious work of finding the relevant parts of the paper that address each claim, dramatically reducing cognitive load.
1429.po: The paper shows that Peerispect can help reviewers, authors, and program committees verify whether review statements are actually grounded in the submission. This creates a practical auditing tool for peer review fairness and allows conference organizers to catch problematic reviews before they influence decisions.

1430.bp: Marketing and advertising often rely on beautiful, persuasive videos to make people want to visit a place or buy a product. Generating these videos at scale is expensive when you need to hire videographers and editors, but automated video generation still struggles with reliability—the generated videos often contain errors or nonsensical visuals that undermine the advertiser's message.
1430.wh: Naive approaches to automated video generation take a description like 'a beach at sunset' and try to generate an entire video at once. This often produces inconsistent results—the sky might change color between frames, or objects might vanish. The system doesn't plan the overall composition or check whether what it generated actually matches what was requested. Video generation is inherently a multi-step problem (choosing themes, generating scenes, checking quality), but most systems try to do it in one shot.
1430.ap: ATVG breaks video generation into a planned sequence of steps: first, it decides what themes or scenes should appear (e.g., landmarks, culture, food for a travel ad); then, for each scene, it retrieves a real image from the internet to use as an anchor point, which constrains the generation to something grounded in reality; it expands that image into a detailed description of the video scene; and finally, it checks the generated video for visual artifacts and errors before assembling the final result. The system works through planning, retrieval, expansion, and verification.
1430.ww: By using real images as anchors, the system grounds its generation in reality—the generated video is constrained to show things that actually exist. By planning before generating, the system ensures thematic consistency across scenes. And by verifying the output, it catches errors before the video reaches customers. Each step reduces the ways the system can go wrong.
1430.po: Testing on real cities shows that ATVG produces more coherent multi-scene videos with better factual accuracy than a simpler baseline. The system can generate travel ads from just a city name, demonstrating that careful agentic planning can overcome the reliability problems that plague naive video generation.

1431.bp: Graphs—data structures showing how things connect to each other (like social networks or knowledge graphs)—are everywhere in real-world applications. Companies and researchers often want to ask questions about groups or communities within these graphs, like 'find all clusters of highly connected users' or 'find groups of products frequently bought together'. Current database systems have no natural way to express these kinds of questions efficiently.
1431.wh: Traditional database query languages work well for finding individual rows or simple patterns, but they struggle with questions about group structure or set-level constraints. If you want to ask 'find all maximal cliques'—groups where everyone is connected to everyone—that's hard to express and slow to compute in standard databases. You end up writing custom code to iterate through the graph manually, which is error-prone and inefficient.
1431.ap: MonacGraph extends a graph query language (Gremlin) with new syntax for reasoning about sets of nodes and their relationships. It introduces monadic second-order logic (MSOL)—a mathematical formalism that lets you write questions like 'find all subsets of nodes where certain properties hold'. The system executes these queries by first evaluating simpler first-order checks efficiently, then combining results to answer the full question. It stores graph structure in a way that precomputes which nodes form communities, so community queries can be answered fast.
1431.ww: By building the query language and storage around the mathematical framework of set-level reasoning, the system makes community queries expressible and efficient. Precomputing community structure means the database doesn't have to re-compute it every time. The web interface lets non-experts write and visualize these queries, making complex graph analysis accessible.
1431.po: MonacGraph demonstrates a working graph database where you can express and execute complex set-level queries on real graph data. This opens up analyses that were previously impractical to express, allowing organizations and researchers to extract insights about community structure and group patterns at scale.

1432.bp: Museums worldwide have digitized their collections—millions of objects described in records, alongside images and historical information. But this data lives in isolated silos: catalog databases, image repositories, and text descriptions don't connect to each other. Visitors and researchers can't easily explore how artifacts relate to each other, who created them, or what cultural connections link different pieces together.
1432.wh: Museum data is heterogeneous—some information is structured (item ID, acquisition date), some is images, and some is free-form text descriptions. Connecting these requires someone to manually build bridges between the different systems, and even then, the data isn't organized in a way that invites exploration. If you find one artifact and wonder 'what else is connected to this?', there's no obvious way to follow those threads.
1432.ap: MuseKG builds a unified graph (a knowledge graph) that brings all these sources together into one queryable structure. Objects, artists, organizations, images, and extracted concepts all become nodes in the graph, and relationships between them become edges. When you ask a natural language question like 'show me works by this artist', the system maps your question to relevant graph entities and returns the connected neighborhood of evidence—the artwork, related objects, biographical context, all linked together.
1432.ww: By unifying heterogeneous data into a typed graph, the system makes relationships explicit and traversable. A visitor can see not just isolated artifacts but how they connect—who created it, what period it's from, what other pieces relate to it. The natural language interface means visitors don't need to learn database query syntax; they just ask.
1432.po: MuseKG supports exploration tasks like attribute lookup ('who made this?'), relation exploration ('what else did this artist create?'), and relation-aware retrieval ('show me pieces from this collection that relate to this theme'). The system makes museum collections legible as a connected whole rather than isolated records.

1433.bp: Recommending food or recipes to people can help nudge them toward healthier eating, but food recommender systems have a problem: unhealthy foods are often more popular and easier to predict, so the system recommends them more often. Even when a system identifies a healthier option, it's hard to explain why that trade-off makes sense in a way that actually convinces people to try it.
1433.wh: Most recommendation systems are trained to predict what users will click or rate highly, which means they learn that people gravitate toward popular foods even if those foods aren't nutritious. Adding explanations helps, but explaining why a salad is better than a burger requires translating dry nutritional data into language that resonates with a user's actual goals and concerns. Testing whether explanations actually change eating behavior requires running studies with real users, which is expensive and technically complex to set up.
1433.ap: XFoodRec is a mobile app that combines recipe recommendations with automatic explanations. The system recommends dishes personalized to your preferences, but when it suggests a healthier option, it uses an AI language model to turn nutritional information into natural-language explanations tailored to the user's health goals. The app also includes built-in A/B testing infrastructure, so researchers can assign users to different explanation styles and measure whether the explanations actually change what people eat.
1433.ww: By personalizing the explanation to the user's stated health goals (e.g., reducing sodium, increasing protein), the system makes the case for healthier food in language the user cares about. By baking A/B testing into the app itself, researchers can measure real behavioral impact without running separate studies—the app automatically logs what recommendations people accept and reject across different explanation styles.
1433.po: XFoodRec bridges the gap between algorithmic recommendation and real-world dietary behavior change. The paper demonstrates that the platform enables researchers to study how different explanation strategies actually influence food choices in practice, not just in simulation.

1434.bp: Researchers reading academic papers often hit moments where a concept is unclear or they want to explore related work, but switching to a search engine breaks their focus and interrupts their reading flow. Ideally, the system could proactively suggest relevant related papers or clarify concepts as they read, without making them leave the document.
1434.wh: Suggesting relevant papers while someone reads sounds simple, but the hard part is knowing what's relevant to them personally. The same paper on neural networks might mean something different to an NLP researcher than to a computer vision researcher—they have different backgrounds, different questions, and different knowledge gaps. A one-size-fits-all suggestion system will generate irrelevant noise. The system needs to understand the reader's background and intent, which isn't visible on the screen.
1434.ap: H-MAPS maintains three layers of memory about the user: a long-term profile (what field are they in?), a reading-session memory (what paper are they reading now?), and a real-time memory (where in the paper are they, and what did they just look at?). When the system detects that you've paused on a concept or section, it uses these three levels of context to infer what you're trying to understand, generates a natural language question that captures your likely information need, and retrieves papers relevant to that specific need. The retrieval happens locally on your device for privacy.
1434.ww: By maintaining hierarchical context, the system can disambiguate what a concept means to this particular reader. The same word triggers different searches for an NLP researcher and an HCI researcher because their profiles are different. By inferring intent from reading behavior (pauses, mouse movements, where you're looking) rather than asking you to type, the system feels proactive rather than intrusive.
1434.po: The paper demonstrates that H-MAPS can generate profile-specific questions and retrieve distinct papers tailored to different users' backgrounds, all triggered by implicit reading behavior. This shows that proactive information retrieval can enhance reading without interrupting the flow.

1435.bp: Large organizations—governments, corporations, law firms—work with regulatory documents and contracts that evolve over time. Each revision produces a new version, but comparing versions manually is incredibly tedious because documents are often hundreds of pages long. Lawyers and auditors need to spot inconsistencies and contradictions introduced by changes, but character-by-character diffs miss the real semantic issues.
1435.wh: Simple diff tools (character-level comparisons) fail when text has been reworded. If a phrase 'this must be reviewed' gets rewritten as 'review is mandatory', a character diff sees them as entirely different, but they mean the same thing. A semantic diff needs to understand that these paraphrases are equivalent. But running semantic comparison on legal text is risky—you need high confidence that your analysis is correct, and you need the system to explain its reasoning.
1435.ap: SLeDoC uses a combination of information-retrieval techniques and large language models to compare legal paragraphs at the semantic level. It identifies corresponding sections between two document versions, then uses language models to judge whether the meaning has changed or merely been reworded. The system goes beyond simple 'same or different' judgments and captures nuances like whether a clause has been strengthened, weakened, or clarified.
1435.ww: By using state-of-the-art language models (which are trained to understand meaning across paraphrases), the system can recognize semantic equivalence even when wording changes. By grounding the comparison in information-retrieval matching, it can handle long documents efficiently. The combination lets the system be both semantically accurate and computationally tractable.
1435.po: SLeDoC was evaluated on a benchmark of legally annotated document pairs, showing that it can accurately detect semantic shifts beyond what character-level tools can achieve. The system makes document auditing practical for legal and compliance professionals, reducing the manual labor required to track changes in complex regulatory texts.

1436.bp: Wikidata is a massive knowledge graph—structured facts about millions of people, places, and concepts. But like all knowledge graphs, it's incomplete. There are billions of true relationships that haven't been added yet because no one has bothered to include them. Identifying missing facts and adding them would make Wikidata more useful, but humans can't manually check every possibility.
1436.wh: Automatically predicting missing relationships in knowledge graphs is possible—there are algorithms (embedding-based models) that can suggest likely connections. But an automated suggestion is only useful if it's grounded in evidence. If the system suggests a fact that's wrong, it pollutes the knowledge graph. And if the suggestion has no evidence, how can a human editor verify it or know whether to trust it?
1436.ap: WikiRAG combines three steps: first, it uses knowledge graph embeddings (a mathematical technique for representing entities as vectors) to suggest candidate relationships; second, it retrieves relevant Wikipedia passages as evidence for each candidate; third, it uses an LLM to assess each candidate by reasoning over the retrieved passages. The system presents candidates alongside their evidence, allowing humans to inspect the reasoning and validate or reject each suggestion before adding it to Wikidata.
1436.ww: By retrieving evidence before asking the LLM to make a judgment, the system ensures that every candidate suggestion comes with grounding in real information. The human-in-the-loop design means the system can be confident (it can suggest high-risk additions) while still letting humans make the final call. This balance reduces both false negatives (missed facts) and false positives (wrong facts added).
1436.po: WikiRAG demonstrates an end-to-end workflow for evidence-based link prediction on Wikidata. The system enables batch validation and export of confirmed triples, making it practical to systematically complete knowledge graphs with human oversight.

1437.bp: When large language models generate long-form text—essays, articles, reports—they sometimes invent facts that sound plausible but are false, a problem called hallucination. Detecting these hallucinations is crucial if you want to use AI for high-stakes applications like writing news articles or research summaries. But existing fact-checking tools are slow, require expensive API calls to external services, and rely on outdated knowledge bases.
1437.wh: Fact-checking long-form text is inherently difficult because you need to verify multiple claims across potentially hundreds of sentences. The obvious approach—checking each claim against a search engine or knowledge base—is slow and expensive if you rely on paid APIs. And if your knowledge base is outdated, you'll miss facts that are actually true. You also need to handle ambiguity (the same name might refer to multiple people) and decide when a paraphrase counts as verification.
1437.ap: FactOWL is a fact-checking tool that decomposes long-form text into individual factual statements, then retrieves evidence from Wikipedia and Wikidata for each statement. It handles ambiguity by checking a statement against multiple Wikipedia pages and aggregating evidence from multiple sources. The system uses open-source language models (not paid APIs) and real-time Wikipedia access (not stale knowledge bases), making it fast and affordable.
1437.ww: By checking each claim against multiple sources and aggregating the results, the system reduces false negatives—it's less likely to call something wrong when it's actually right. Using open-source models and real-time Wikipedia means the system is fast (because it avoids API latency) and stays current. The multi-source approach also helps resolve entity ambiguity by seeing which page actually supports the claim.
1437.po: FactOWL is at least 10× faster than the prior state-of-the-art fact-checking tool (FActScore) and is freely available. The paper demonstrates that efficient, open-source fact-checking is now practical, enabling researchers and practitioners to verify LLM outputs without expensive infrastructure.

1438.bp: Trademark protection requires examining whether a new trademark might be confused with existing ones—the 'likelihood of confusion' test. This is a complex judgment involving visual similarity, pronunciation, conceptual meaning, and the types of goods being sold. Lawyers currently search for conflicting trademarks manually and make these judgments themselves, which is slow and subjective. Could AI help systematize this reasoning?
1438.wh: A simple ranked list of similar existing trademarks isn't enough for trademark clearance because the judgment isn't just 'which marks are most similar?' but 'for these specific candidate marks, is there a real risk of consumer confusion across all these dimensions?'. This requires weighing multiple factors (appearance, sound, concept, goods), resolving edge cases (is a generic symbol confusable?), and producing a clear risk score. A retrieval system gives you candidates, but the real work is comparative judgment across multiple dimensions under the examination rules.
1438.ap: T-RADAR uses agentic simulation to handle this multi-dimensional judgment. First, it retrieves potentially conflicting trademarks using multimodal search (visual and semantic similarity). Then, instead of just ranking, it simulates an adversarial examination between a mock Examiner and an Applicant, where they debate the visual, phonetic, conceptual, and goods-related aspects of similarity. The simulation produces a Conflict Risk score and Registrability score based on this debate.
1438.ww: By simulating the actual examination process (rather than trying to predict the score directly), the system can capture the nuanced reasoning that trademark examiners use. The adversarial format means the system has to consider counterarguments—both why marks might be confused and why they might not be. When multiple candidates are tested, comparing their simulated outcomes reveals high-risk pairs.
1438.po: T-RADAR demonstrates that agentic simulation can be used as an interface for complex, multi-criteria judgment. The system produces interpretable risk scores that serve as review prioritization signals, helping lawyers focus their effort on the genuinely risky cases.

1439.bp: Researchers and students often read mathematical papers and articles filled with formulas and equations, but standard PDF readers treat math as just pixels on a page—you can't search for formulas, click on an equation to find related work, or ask the system to explain a derivation. This isolation of mathematical notation from the rest of the text creates a barrier to exploration and learning.
1439.wh: Mathematical content is hard to index and search because formulas are visual structures—a Laplace transform looks like a series of symbols on the page, but there's no underlying text to search for. Standard full-text search is useless for math. Meanwhile, specialized math search tools exist but they're separate from PDF readers, forcing readers to switch windows and lose context. The tools and document viewers exist in silos.
1439.ap: MathMex-PDF integrates mathematical extraction and multimodal retrieval into a single PDF reader. It processes PDF pages to detect where formulas are, recognizes the mathematical notation (converting pixel images into structured representations like LaTeX), and grounds those formulas in the document layout. You can then search using natural language ('find the convolution operator'), LaTeX (' find \\ast'), or mixed queries, and click on any rendered formula to trigger a reverse search that finds related papers containing similar formulas.
1439.ww: By recognizing and indexing formulas alongside text, the system makes mathematical content discoverable in the same workflow as text. By supporting multiple query types (natural language, LaTeX, hybrid, query-by-example), it meets users where they are. By applying reciprocal rank fusion to combine formula and text rankings, it weights both modalities appropriately.
1439.po: MathMex-PDF demonstrates unified math-text retrieval in an interactive PDF reader, making it practical to explore mathematical content without leaving the document. The system also provides accessibility features like spoken-math annotations, helping readers with visual impairments engage with mathematical papers.
